about.title: About me
about.bio1: I'm a freelance full-stack developer with a strong backend focus. I build web applications and tools — mostly with Go on the server and SvelteKit on the frontend — and I care about systems that are fast, simple, and correct.
about.bio2: My main stack is Go and Svelte. I reach for Python or Rust when the problem calls for it. I'm comfortable with the tooling that gets a vision to production — Docker, PostgreSQL, Ansible, Terraform — and I self-host wherever it makes sense, both for privacy and to keep costs down. AI-augmented development is part of how I work — I use it to move faster on well-scoped problems, not to replace the judgment behind them.
about.bio3: I studied mathematics up through graduate coursework, which probably explains why I'm drawn to things like consensus algorithms and encryption. Outside of code, I tinker with electronics and play electric guitar.

cluo.overview_1: Built to replace manual investigation workflows. Field agents use a Wails + SvelteKit desktop app for case management, capture evidence on a mobile PWA, and deliver securely to clients through a dedicated portal — all driven by one Go API.
cluo.overview_2: The legal document chain (Estimate → Mandate → Contract → Invoice) is automated as a state machine with per-document PDF generation.
cluo.highlight_1_body: Go API, Wails desktop, mobile PWA, and client portal all share a single hexagonal backend with port interfaces.
cluo.highlight_2_body: transcribes field audio, extracts structured data (people, timelines, facts), and pre-fills the report editor.
cluo.highlight_3_body: Estimate → Mandate → Contract → Invoice modeled as a state machine with per-document PDF generation and delivery.
cluo.highlight_4_body: SHA-256 tokens with configurable expiration and investigator-controlled revocation — no client accounts needed.
cluo.highlight_5_body: Ansible + Terraform for reproducible, version-controlled deployments.

leviosa.overview_1: A crucial component originally built for another project, extracted as a standalone library to facilitate encryption and hashing of sensitive data. The main challenge was designing an API that stays out of the way while remaining correct and fast.
leviosa.learned_1: Leviosa was my first real backend project, built in a language I was learning at the same time. I came from HTML, CSS, and JavaScript — no servers, no databases, no type systems. Go was a deliberate choice: I wanted to understand how software actually runs. The Learn Go with Tests book was my entry point, and it was the first time I thought seriously about correctness, not just about making something work.
leviosa.learned_2: One of the earliest conceptual breakthroughs was understanding the client-server model properly. I had a SvelteKit frontend, a SvelteKit backend, and a Go API running in parallel, and I couldn't reason about how they communicated. The insight that unlocked it: client and server are not fixed, physical roles — they're contextual. The same machine can be a server to a browser and a client to another service depending on who initiates the request. That shift changed how I model every distributed system I've built since.
leviosa.learned_3: I also reached for complexity before I'd earned it. Stripe, Vault, and RabbitMQ went into the project because they appeared on job descriptions, not because I fully understood what problems they solved. The most demanding conceptual wall was the DEK/KEK encryption model: understanding why two layers of keys exist, and why that architecture makes key rotation cheap rather than catastrophic. The pattern felt arbitrary until it became necessary — and that gap between 'I implemented it' and 'I understood it' is what this project taught me to close.
leviosa.learned_4: Debugging without AI meant reading Go stack traces manually — learning to find the panicking goroutine, read frame order, and form one hypothesis at a time. I also learned to step away. The bugs that resisted hours of pressure often yielded in minutes with fresh eyes. Architecturally, the modular monolith was not an upfront design decision: I started with a flat structure, considered microservices, found the operational overhead too costly for a solo developer, and arrived at bounded modules as the right tradeoff. Most of my best architectural decisions came from feeling the cost of the wrong one first.

germinal.tagline: Event & talent management platform with bilingual support, media galleries, and automated workflows.
germinal.overview_1: A sophisticated event and talent management platform with bilingual support, media galleries, automated workflows, and production-ready infrastructure.
germinal.overview_2: Built from the ground up as a full-stack showcase demonstrating modern web development practices. The platform features a custom middleware system for cross-cutting concerns, an LRU caching layer with tag-based invalidation, and a PostgreSQL-backed job scheduler for asynchronous tasks.
germinal.highlight_1_body: Decorator pattern for composable request handling — validation, auth, rate limiting, and CSRF in a single chain.
germinal.highlight_2_body: pg-boss integration with cron-scheduled tasks for email queues, cleanup, and reminders.
germinal.highlight_3_body: LRU cache with TTL and tag-based invalidation for optimal performance.
germinal.highlight_4_body: End-to-end TypeScript with Zod schemas for runtime validation.
germinal.highlight_5_body: Multi-stage Docker builds with security hardening (non-root user, Alpine base).
germinal.highlight_6_body: Sentry integration for error tracking and performance monitoring.
germinal.highlight_7_body: Vitest for unit tests and Playwright for E2E coverage.
germinal.learned_1: Germinal was technically more complex than anything I'd built before — middleware chains, background jobs, LRU caching, production Docker, Sentry, Playwright. But it was easier to build. That gap is the most honest measure of growth: the complexity that would have overwhelmed me in an earlier project was the complexity I chose deliberately here, because I'd developed enough of a mental model to reach for the right tools at the right time.
germinal.learned_2: The hardest part was the background job system. Asynchronous work introduces a class of bugs that doesn't exist in synchronous code — jobs that fail silently, jobs that succeed but produce wrong side effects, jobs that appear scheduled but never run. Sentry was what finally made those failures visible. Before adding observability, I was reasoning about system behavior from the outside; after, I could see exactly what was happening. That experience made observability non-negotiable in everything I build.
germinal.learned_3: My relationship with tests changed significantly on this project. Earlier, tests felt like a liability: if your architecture is still in flux, maintaining tests through refactors costs more than they save. Germinal was stable enough that the cost inverted. I lean toward integration tests rather than unit tests — they survive internal refactors, they test behavior rather than implementation, and in a full-stack application they're the closest thing to a guarantee that the system actually works.
germinal.learned_4: This was also the project where I shifted from writing code by hand to working with AI as part of my workflow. The first version of that shift created cognitive debt — I'd delegate implementation and find myself holding code I didn't fully own. The bugs I couldn't debug were almost always in code I hadn't written with enough intention. What changed was precision: learning to direct AI at specific problems rather than broad features, and letting the existing codebase patterns guide both the AI and me toward consistent decisions.
germinal.learned_5: Finishing Germinal — deploying it completely, with production infrastructure, as a solo developer — is what I'm most proud of across all my projects. Finishing is underrated. Most projects die before deployment, not because the code is too hard but because the final stretch — hardening, monitoring, the unsexy work — doesn't have the momentum of building features. Crossing that line changed how I think about what it means to ship software.

encx.overview_1: A crucial component of the Cluo project that facilitates encryption and hashing of sensitive data. Designed as a standalone module to avoid becoming a bottleneck in the data pipeline.
encx.learned_1: ENCX started as a pain point inside another project. I had encryption and hashing operations spread across many struct handlers, and because my understanding of cryptography was still developing, I kept making the same mistakes in different places. One wrong algorithm choice, replicated five times, means five refactors. The solution was extraction: pull the crypto logic into a library, get it right once, and let everything else depend on that.
encx.learned_2: Building a library forced a kind of understanding that just using code doesn't. When you write something for a caller you're not standing next to, you have to answer questions you can otherwise ignore: what does the caller need to know? What should they never be able to touch? That discipline — thinking from the outside of your own code — is something I now apply to every module I build.
encx.learned_3: The hardest design decision was how opinionated to be. I chose to hide the algorithm entirely: callers encrypt and hash, they don't select primitives. The defaults are correct. That choice came directly from my own past mistakes — I was the caller who had picked wrong algorithms — and it produced a principle I've carried into every API since: a good interface makes the wrong thing hard to do.

vizraft.overview_1: VizRaft is a from-scratch implementation of the Raft distributed consensus algorithm in Go, paired with a real-time visualizer that makes the protocol's behavior tangible. Leader elections, log replication, and network partition recovery all play out visually as you interact with the cluster.
vizraft.overview_2: The goal is to turn a paper into running code, then make that code explainable — both to myself and to anyone trying to understand how distributed systems stay consistent under failure.
